guideTitle: 6 Best Garden Augers for Bulbs in 2026
metaTitle: Best Garden Augers for Bulbs in 2026
metaDescription: Six bulb-planting auger bits compared by diameter, length, and set options, so you can plant tulips and daffodils faster without kneeling in the dirt.
introParagraphs: Planting bulbs is one of those garden chores that sounds pleasant until you face a few hundred of them. Each one needs its own hole at the right depth, and a hand trowel means a lot of kneeling, twisting, and sore knuckles. A bulb auger flips that job around by letting a cordless drill do the digging while you stand and guide it, so the work becomes a steady rhythm of drill, drop, and move on.

For bulbs specifically, the diameter and length of the bit matter more than raw power. A narrow bit near 1.6 inches suits crocus and small bulbs, a 2 to 3 inch bit handles tulips and daffodils, and longer shafts let you reach the correct planting depth without bending. We evaluated six options based on product specs and buyer feedback, weighing how well each matches typical bulb holes rather than just how large the number on the box is.
The lineup includes single bits, a four-piece set, and a two-pack, so you can match your collection to the way you actually plant.

products.name: MAXCCINO 2x14.5 Bulb Auger
products.description:
The MAXCCINO 2x14.5 is the most balanced single bit for bulb work. Two inches of diameter makes a hole wide enough for most tulips and daffodils with a little room to backfill, and 14.5 inches of length easily clears the depth most bulbs need. The maker describes an upgraded bit with more blades on the shaft, which is meant to lift soil more efficiently per turn.

The 3/8 inch non-slip drive fits any chucked drill, and the listing recommends an 18V or higher drill. That is an honest requirement: a weaker drill will bog down in heavy soil even with a narrow bit. The tradeoff of this size is that it is not ideal for very small bulbs, where a 1.6 inch bit leaves a tidier hole, and it is too narrow for potted plants.

For ownership, the manufacturer advises keeping the auger clean of soil and debris when not in use, which is easy with a quick rinse. Compared with the TCBWFY and Sproot at 1.6 inches, it moves more soil per pass, and compared with the Power Planter at 3 inches, it creates a smaller, more bulb-appropriate hole. If you want one bit for a mixed spring planting, this is the one to start with, ideally with a side handle on your drill.

cons: Too narrow for potted plants and larger plantings
Needs an 18V or stronger drill in heavy soil

products.name: TCBWFY 1.6x16.5 Bulb Auger
products.description:
The TCBWFY 1.6x16.5 is the narrow, long option built for small bulbs. A 1.6 inch diameter is just right for crocus, snowdrops, grape hyacinths, and similar bulbs, where a wider hole wastes soil and loosens the surrounding bed. The solid shaft carries more spirals than a basic bit, and the extended 16.5 inch length lets you plant while standing.

That length is the real benefit. The listing notes it is meant to spare you from bending low, and a 16.5 inch reach clears the depth for both small and medium bulbs. The tradeoff is the narrow bore: you will struggle to fit a large daffodil or a fat tulip without enlarging the hole. Heavy-duty steel with black paint holds up to repeated use but will show scuffs after contact with stones.

Day to day, this bit rinses clean and stores easily thanks to its slim profile. Compared with the Sproot 1.6x16.5, it is the same size, so choose between them on listing details and finish, and compared with the MAXCCINO at 2 inches, it is better for small bulbs but less flexible. It is also a lighter load on the drill than the wider options, which matters if your cordless drill is modest. Use a side handle and pulse the trigger to keep it from binding.
products.bestFor: Planting small bulbs like crocus and grape hyacinth while standing up.
pros: Narrow 1.6 inch hole suits crocus and other small bulbs
Sixteen and a half inches lets you plant standing
Solid shaft with extra spirals clears soil steadily
Slim profile puts less load on a modest drill
cons: Bore is too narrow for large daffodils and fat tulips

products.name: MAXCCINO 4-Piece Auger Set
products.description:
The MAXCCINO 4-Piece Auger Set is the choice when your garden contains more than one kind of bulb or planting job. It contains four sizes: 1.6 by 8.6 inches, 3 by 12 inches, 2 by 14.5 inches, and 2.6 by 16.5 inches, each with a 3/8 inch non-slip drive. The listing mentions the same upgraded design with more blades on the shaft as the single MAXCCINO bit.

That range lets you use a short, narrow bit for crocus, a 2 inch bit for tulips, and a wider 3 inch bit for potted perennials or larger bulbs. It also means you can mix tasks in one afternoon without buying separately. The tradeoff is storage and sorting: four bits take more room, and you will need to keep them clean and organized so you do not grab the wrong one in the middle of planting.

The maker recommends an 18V or higher drill and advises keeping the augers clear of soil and debris. Compared with the single MAXCCINO 2x14.5, you get the same 2 inch size plus three other options, and compared with the NAFOGAR two-pack, you get two more sizes to choose from. If you are buying your first bulb auger and you are unsure of your needs, this set removes the guesswork about diameter.

products.name: Sproot 1.6x16.5 Bulb Auger
products.description:
The Sproot 1.6x16.5 shares its dimensions with the TCBWFY, but its listing highlights a different feature: an extended spiral that is meant to dig deeper, cleaner holes. The spiral runs farther up the shaft, which helps carry soil out of the hole instead of leaving it to fall back in. It uses a standard 3/8 inch hex drive and is sold as a single bit without a drill.

That design is useful in beds with looser soil, where fallen-back dirt can clog the hole and slow planting. It still shares the 1.6 inch limitation of being narrow, so it works best for crocus, snowdrops, and similar small bulbs rather than large tulips. The listing also notes it can be used for bedding plants and holes for fence posts, umbrellas, ground lights, and outdoor decor, though those jobs generally suit wider bits.

In ownership, it is easy to rinse and store, and the plain design has no moving parts to fail. Compared with the TCBWFY 1.6x16.5, it is nearly identical in size, so pick based on which listing and spiral description you trust more. Compared with the NAFOGAR two-pack, which includes a 1.6x16.5 bit plus a wider one, it gives you a single bit at the same size. A side handle and low-speed, high-torque drill setting will give the cleanest results.
products.bestFor: Planters who want a clean, narrow, deep hole in loose beds.
pros: Extended spiral carries soil up and out of the hole
Sixteen and a half inches reaches proper depth for small bulbs
Standard 3/8 inch hex shank fits ordinary drills

cons: Narrow 1.6 inch bore cannot fit larger bulbs

products.name: NAFOGAR 2-Pack Auger Set
products.description:
The NAFOGAR 2-Pack gives you two sizes at the extremes of bulb and bedding work: a slim 1.6 by 16.5 inch bit and a wide 3.5 by 16 inch bit. The small one handles crocus and similar bulbs, while the 3.5 inch one makes a hole for larger bulbs, perennials, or seedlings. Both attach to a standard 3/8 inch hex drill, and the maker sells them as a value pack for gardeners who want more than one size.

The range is the main strength. Many gardeners find that one bit is not enough, and a narrow plus wide combination covers a lot of ground without the bulk of a four-piece set. The tradeoff is that you skip the middle size around 2 to 3 inches, which is the most common bulb hole, so tulips and daffodils will either use the wider bit or require a separate purchase.

Ownership is simple. Each bit rinses clean and stores easily, and the heavy-duty steel is meant to last across seasons. Compared with the MAXCCINO set, it offers fewer sizes but at a simpler grouping, and compared with the single Sproot 1.6x16.5, it adds a wide option for larger holes. Use a drill with a side handle, because the 3.5 inch bit needs real torque and will punish a weak drill.
products.bestFor: Gardeners who want one tiny bit and one wide bit for varied planting.
pros: Two sizes at 1.6 and 3.5 inches cover small and large holes
Both bits are about 16 inches long for standing work
Standard 3/8 inch hex drive fits ordinary drills
Simpler to store than a four-piece set
cons: Skips the common 2 to 3 inch size for tulips
The 3.5 inch bit needs a strong drill to avoid stalling

products.name: Power Planter DIY Guru 3x12 Auger
products.description:
The Power Planter DIY Guru 3x12 is the broader, shorter auger in this lineup. At 3 inches wide and 12 inches long, it digs a hole suited to bigger bulbs, small perennials, and bedding plants rather than tiny crocus bulbs. The maker presents it as an alternative to post-hole diggers, bulb planters, or shovels, and says its patent-pending design is effective in dirt, clay, rocky soil, and sand.

That soil claim is the reason to choose it. If your garden has stubborn ground, a wider, sturdier design with a shorter shaft can feel more stable than a long, thin bit that flexes. The same listing notes uses beyond planting, including paint and cement mixing, which is not what most gardeners need but shows how sturdy the design is meant to be. The tradeoff is that a 3 inch hole is too large for small bulbs, and 12 inches limits depth for deep plantings.

In ownership, it handles like a compact tool that stores easily and wipes clean. Compared with the MAXCCINO 2x14.5, it digs a wider hole but with less depth, and compared with the TCBWFY 1.6x16.5, it is built for bulk rather than precision. Check the chuck size on the listing before you order, and use a side handle with a drill strong enough to turn a 3 inch bore.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Bulb size should set the bit diameter, because a hole that is too wide wastes effort and one that is too narrow squeezes the bulb. A 1.6 inch bit like the TCBWFY 1.6x16.5 or Sproot 1.6x16.5 suits crocus, snowdrops, and grape hyacinths. The MAXCCINO 2x14.5 handles most tulips and daffodils, while the Power Planter 3x12 and the NAFOGAR 3.5 inch bit suit large bulbs and small perennials. Measure your biggest bulb across its widest point and choose a bit at least a half inch wider.

Most bulbs go in at a depth of roughly two to three times their height, which means many tulips and daffodils need holes of 6 to 8 inches. A bit around 14 to 16 inches, like the MAXCCINO 2x14.5 at 14.5 inches or the TCBWFY and Sproot at 16.5 inches, lets you dig that depth while standing. A short bit such as the Power Planter at 12 inches works for shallower plantings. Longer is only useful if you will actually use the reach, otherwise it adds leverage and wrist strain.

Choose a set if you plant several kinds of bulbs, since one diameter rarely fits all of them. The MAXCCINO 4-Piece Auger Set covers 1.6, 2, 2.6, and 3 inch diameters, and the NAFOGAR 2-Pack gives a 1.6 and 3.5 inch pair. A single bit like the MAXCCINO 2x14.5 is simpler and easier to store. If you only plant tulips, one bit is enough, but mixed beds benefit from the set.

Even narrow bits need enough drill to turn through soil. The MAXCCINO listings recommend an 18V or higher drill, and wider bits like the 3.5 inch NAFOGAR or the 3 inch Power Planter benefit from 20V and a side handle. Clay stalls weak drills fast, and a clutch helps by slipping if the bit catches. Use low speed and high torque, and pulse the trigger instead of leaning on the drill.

Most bulb augers use a 3/8 inch hex or non-slip shank that fits any chucked drill, including the MAXCCINO, TCBWFY, Sproot, and NAFOGAR picks. A hex shank grips the chuck flats instead of slipping under load. The Power Planter DIY Guru listing does not spell out the shank size in its bullets, so confirm it before buying. If you plan to use a larger auger later, check the shank size against your drill now.

Soil type changes what works best. Loose beds suit a long, narrow bit like the Sproot 1.6x16.5 with its extended spiral, while clay and rocky ground suit the Power Planter 3x12, which is listed for dirt, clay, rocky soil, and sand. Wet clay sticks to flighting, so clear it often. A pointed tip helps the bit start without walking across the surface.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hole size for bulbs
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each diameter to typical bulb sizes, from small bulbs at 1.6 inches to larger ones at 3 inches and above. The TCBWFY and Sproot lead for small bulbs, the MAXCCINO 2x14.5 leads for mid-size bulbs, and the Power Planter 3x12 leads for large ones. A bit that fits a wide range of bulbs earned higher marks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach for standing work
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on product specs, we compared length against the depth bulbs need and the comfort of planting without bending. The TCBWFY and Sproot at 16.5 inches reach farthest, the MAXCCINO at 14.5 inches sits in the middle, and the Power Planter at 12 inches is shortest. We rewarded lengths that stay controllable rather than extreme.

howWeEvaluated.title: Variety and flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: Gardeners rarely plant just one bulb type, so we looked at whether a pick offers multiple sizes. The MAXCCINO 4-Piece Auger Set offers four, the NAFOGAR 2-Pack offers two, and the other picks are single bits. Sets earned extra credit for flexibility, with a small note for the storage they require.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drill demands
howWeEvaluated.description: We reviewed how much drill each bit asks for, using manufacturer guidance and buyer feedback. The MAXCCINO listings call for 18V or higher, and wider bits like the NAFOGAR 3.5 inch need more torque still. Slimmer bits such as the TCBWFY 1.6x16.5 place the lightest load on a modest drill.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and ease of ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered materials, finishes, and how easy each bit is to clean and store. Heavy-duty steel with paint is common across the picks, and the Power Planter adds a soil-type claim for clay and rock. All of them rinse clean, but sets and longer bits need more storage space, which we factored in.

faq.q: What size auger is best for tulips and daffodils?
faq.a: A 2 inch bit like the MAXCCINO 2x14.5 is the best match for most tulips and daffodils. It makes a hole wide enough for the bulb with a little room to backfill. Larger bulbs may need a 3 inch bit like the Power Planter 3x12. Measure the widest bulb in your bag before choosing.

faq.q: How deep should I plant bulbs with an auger?
faq.a: A common rule is to plant bulbs about two to three times their height deep. That puts many tulips and daffodils at roughly 6 to 8 inches. A 14 to 16 inch bit reaches that easily without you bending. Mark the depth on the shaft with tape so every hole is consistent.

faq.q: What drill do I need for a bulb auger?
faq.a: An 18V or higher cordless drill is recommended for the MAXCCINO bits. Wider bits like the NAFOGAR 3.5 inch or the Power Planter 3x12 are easier with a 20V drill and a side handle. A drill with a clutch is safer if the bit catches a root. Use low speed and high torque.

faq.q: Is a set better than a single bit?
faq.a: A set is better if you plant several kinds of bulbs, because no single diameter fits everything. The MAXCCINO 4-Piece Auger Set covers 1.6 to 3 inches, and the NAFOGAR 2-Pack covers a narrow and a wide size. A single bit is simpler and easier to store. If you plant mostly one kind of bulb, a single bit is enough.

faq.q: Will an auger work in clay soil?
faq.a: Yes, but it needs a stronger drill and more patience. The Power Planter DIY Guru 3x12 is listed for dirt, clay, rocky soil, and sand. Wet clay clings to the flighting, so pulse the trigger and clear the bit often. If the drill stalls repeatedly, step down to a narrower bit.

faq.q: Do I need to clean the auger after use?
faq.a: Yes, a quick rinse and dry after use keeps the bit working well. The MAXCCINO maker advises keeping the auger clean of soil and debris. Paint and coatings chip over time, so bare steel can rust if stored wet. A light oil wipe before winter helps.

faq.q: Can I plant bulbs upside down by mistake with an auger?
faq.a: It is a common worry because holes are narrow and you cannot see the bottom. Drop each bulb pointed end up, and use a long stick or your finger to check its orientation. A wider bit like the MAXCCINO 2x14.5 makes this easier than a slim 1.6 inch hole. Once covered, most bulbs will still find their way up if slightly off.
